newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries retreat as fears of Fed hike rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries retreat as fears of Fed hike rise.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed substantially lower on Tuesday after two consecutive days of ample gains, as fears of an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve continued to mount.

The lion's share of the price damage came in the wake of comments from Fed Governor Janet Yellen, who told Reuters in an interview that the U.S. economy had entered into an "inflationary danger zone."
Yellen also characterized U.S. labor market conditions as "quite tight," and stressed the need for a forward-looking monetary policy.
Because she is perceived to be one of the more dovish members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), Yellen's somewhat "hawkish" comments surprised the market, economists said.
"The Yellen comments were the catalyst," said Lee Youngdahl, money market economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc.
"You may get (some FOMC members) on the dissenting side, but it seems like the core consensus is beginning to form around a 25 basis point cautionary move (on September 24)."
The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond closed at 95-17/32, off 15/32 on the day to yield 7.11 percent. The 6.125 percent two-year note ended down 2/32 at 99-20/32 to yield 6.33 percent.

Economists said a Commerce Department report on wholesale inventories and sales as well as the Richmond Federal Reserve Bank's monthly manufacturing and services survey also contributed to the negative price tilt.

Inventories registered growth of 0.1 percent in July versus a revised gain of 0.2 percent in June. The Richmond Fed manufacturing shipments index rose to 16 in August versus a minus seven reading in July.
A series of market-friendly second-tier releases on retail sales and productivity were overshadowed by Yellen's comments and had little tangible impact on prices, economists said.

The BTM/Schroders chain store sales index fell 1.7 percent in the week ended September 7, while the Redbook retail sales index rose 0.1 percent on a month-to-month basis in the first week of September.

The Labor Department reported that U.S. non-farm productivity grew at a 0.5 percent pace in the second quarter, versus a 0.1 percent decline in its first estimate. Second quarter unit labor cost growth was revised to 3.2 percent from an original reading of 3.8 percent.

"I think the market expected the unit labor cost number to drop and productivity to rise so it wasn't enough of a positive surprise to keep the market going, and we had had a pretty extensive rally for two days," said John Spinello, government bond strategist at Merrill Lynch Government Securities Inc.

The three-month Treasury bill closed up one basis point at 5.15 percent, the six-month bill ended up three basis points at 5.33 percent and the one-year bill was up three at 5.58 percent. The Treasury's 6.5 percent five-year note ended down 5/32 at 99-06/32 to yield 6.69 percent, and the 7.0 percent 10-year note fell 10/32 to 100-16/32, yielding 6.93 percent.
